introduction: On this Sunday, Abraham bargains boldly with God for the city of Sodom, asking him to spare it for the sake of the righteous. In the Gospel, Jesus teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer and tells them to ask, seek and knock, for the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Paul tells us that God has forgiven all our sins. Let us pray with persistence and trust.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, Jesus taught us to call God our Father. With confidence, let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may be a praying community, persistent and full of trust. Let us pray to the Lord.
For cities and nations where evil seems to prevail: that the prayers of the righteous may obtain God's mercy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have stopped praying because their prayers seemed unanswered: that they may keep asking, seeking and knocking. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who lack their daily bread: that they may receive what they need. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that the Father may give us the Holy Spirit, his greatest gift. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Our Father in heaven, your Son taught us to pray and promised that you will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Hear our prayers, forgive us our sins, and lead us in your way. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Lord, teach us to pray
reflection.body:
Abraham's conversation with God in the first reading is one of the boldest prayers in the Bible. God is about to judge Sodom, and Abraham steps forward: "Will you consume the righteous with the wicked?" He bargains: what if there are fifty righteous people? Forty-five? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Ten? Each time God agrees. Abraham knows he is only "dust and ashes," but he speaks to God with daring, because he trusts in God's justice and mercy.

In the Gospel, Jesus has been praying, and one of his disciples asks, "Lord, teach us to pray." Jesus gives them the Lord's Prayer, in the short form that Luke records. It begins with God: "Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come." Then it brings our needs: daily bread, forgiveness, protection from temptation.

Then Jesus tells a story about persistence. A man knocks on his friend's door at midnight to borrow bread for an unexpected guest. The friend does not want to get up, but he does "because of his persistence." And Jesus says: "keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you."

Then he points to the heart of the Father. No father would give his child a snake instead of a fish. "If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?" The greatest answer to prayer is the gift of God himself.

Paul reminds us that we pray as forgiven people: God has forgiven all our trespasses, "nailing it to the cross."

This week, pray the Our Father slowly each day, word by word. And bring one intention to God with persistence, like Abraham, like the friend at midnight.
